title: Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
summary: Writing from prison, Paul greets Philemon and the church in his house and thanks God for Philemon's love. He then appeals, rather than commands, on behalf of Onesimus, Philemon's slave, who has become a believer through Paul. Paul sends him back, asks Philemon to receive him as a beloved brother, offers to pay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room, hoping to be released and to visit soon.
story: The book of Acts ends with Paul under guard awaiting trial, and his letters from prison show what he was doing there: writing, praying, and making disciples of whoever came near. One of those disciples was Onesimus, a slave from a Christian household in Colossae. His conversion creates a problem that no sermon could solve on its own. He legally belongs to Philemon, a leader in the church, and he is away from his master's house, possibly in serious trouble. This letter is Paul's attempt to bring the two men back together as brothers without pretending the wrong or the risk away. It sits beside Colossians, which was likely carried on the same trip and which names Onesimus as a faithful and beloved brother (Colossians 4:9).
historical:
Paul identifies himself only as a prisoner, and the place is uncertain. If he writes from Rome, the date is around AD 60 to 62; if from Ephesus, around AD 53 to 55; a few suggest Caesarea, around AD 57 to 59. His companions are known from elsewhere. Timothy was his long-time co-worker. Epaphras founded the church at Colossae (Colossians 1:7). Mark is John Mark, once the cause of Paul's split with Barnabas (Acts 15:37-39) and now restored to his circle. Aristarchus came from Thessalonica and traveled with Paul to Rome (Acts 27:2). Luke is the physician traditionally credited with the Gospel and Acts, and Demas would later leave Paul (2 Timothy 4:10).

What Onesimus had done is not stated. Verse 18 raises the possibility that he had wronged Philemon or owed him something, and the traditional reading is that he ran away, perhaps with stolen money. Some scholars point to a distinction in Roman legal writings between a fugitive and a slave who went to a friend of his master to ask for intercession in a dispute, and suggest Onesimus went looking for Paul for that reason. Others think Philemon had sent him to help Paul. Each view explains some details and strains at others. The Roman writer Pliny the Younger, in the early second century, wrote a well-known letter to a friend named Sabinianus pleading for a freedman who had offended him, which shows that such intercession letters were a recognized social practice.
cultural:
Churches in the first century met in homes, and a house church gathered the household itself: family members, slaves, freedmen, and neighbors. Addressing the letter to Apphia, Archippus, and the whole church means that Philemon will hear it read in front of the very people whose opinion matters to him, including, perhaps, Onesimus. Paul's request is private in subject and public in setting, and that is deliberate.

Roman slavery was legal ownership of a human being. A master could punish, sell, or free a slave, and runaways faced harsh penalties. Freeing slaves was common, and freed slaves often remained in a relationship of obligation to their former owners. The name Onesimus means useful or beneficial and was a common slave name, the kind of name an owner gives. Paul plays on it: Onesimus was once "useless" (achrestos) and is now "useful" (euchrestos), a pun that may also echo Christos, which was pronounced much like chrestos in that period. Paul's language of fatherhood (verse 10), heart (verses 7, 12, 20), partnership (verse 17), and account-keeping (verses 18-19) draws on family, friendship, and commerce, the three great bonds of the ancient world.
literary: The letter follows the standard shape of an ancient letter (greeting, thanksgiving, body, closing), but every part serves the appeal. The thanksgiving (verses 4-7) praises Philemon for refreshing "the hearts of the saints", and the body closes by asking him to "Refresh my heart in Christ" (verse 20). Paul delays naming Onesimus until verse 10, after he has described himself as aged and in chains. He moves from what he could command (verse 8) to what he chooses to ask (verse 9), from sending (verse 12) to what he would rather have done (verse 13), and from debt (verse 18) to the greater debt Philemon owes him (verse 19). Ancient teachers of rhetoric would have recognized the techniques: winning goodwill, appealing to emotion, and presenting the requested action as honorable. The request for a guest room in verse 22 is not an afterthought; it means Paul intends to see for himself how Onesimus was received.

outline.t: Greeting to Philemon and the church in his house
Thanksgiving for Philemon's faith and love
An appeal of love for Onesimus, once useless, now useful
Sent back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother
Receive him as me; charge his debt to my account
Confidence in Philemon and a request for a guest room
Greetings from Paul's companions and a blessing

doctrines.note: The letter shows what the church does to the social order within it. Master and slave meet as brothers in one house church, and Paul asks that their new relationship "in the Lord" govern their relationship "in person" as well (verse 16).

Paul does not preach the atonement here, but he enacts its logic. He stands between the offended party and the offender, takes the debt on himself, and asks that the offender be received as he would be received. Christians have long read this as a living picture of Christ's work.
Paul calls Onesimus his child, whose father he became in prison (verse 10), and asks Philemon to receive him as a brother. Faith creates a family that crosses the lines of law, class, and household.

words.note: Onesimos, Onesimus, from a Greek word meaning profit or benefit. It was a common slave name, a label chosen for usefulness to an owner. Paul turns the name into a promise: the man who had failed to live up to it is now truly useful, to Philemon and to Paul (verse 11).

Doulos, slave. The ordinary word for a person owned by another. Paul uses the same word for himself elsewhere (a slave of Christ Jesus, Romans 1:1). Here he writes that Onesimus returns no longer merely as a doulos but above one, as a brother (verse 16). The sentence does not abolish the legal category, but it refuses to let the category be the last word about the man.

Koinonia, partnership, fellowship, sharing. Paul prays that Philemon's koinonia of faith will be effective (verse 6), and then asks in verse 17 whether Philemon counts him a koinonos, a partner. The word joins shared faith with shared life and even shared financial obligation, which is exactly the point Paul is pressing.

Splanchna, literally the inner organs, used for the seat of the deepest feelings, much as English uses heart. It appears three times: Philemon has refreshed the splanchna of the saints (verse 7), Onesimus is Paul's very splanchna (verse 12), and Paul asks Philemon to refresh his splanchna (verse 20).

christ: The letter shows what union with Christ does to people who were divided by law and power. Paul's phrases "in Christ" and "in the Lord" are not decoration; they are the ground of every request. Because Onesimus is now in Christ, he is Paul's child and Philemon's brother, and Philemon owes him a welcome that the law never required. Paul's offer, "charge it to my account", has long been read as a picture of Christ, who takes on the debt of those who have wronged God and asks that they be received as he himself is received. Martin Luther made the comparison in his preface to the letter, saying in effect that we are all Christ's Onesimus. The comparison is an analogy drawn from Paul's theology, not a hidden meaning in the text, but it is a fitting one.

hard.q: Why doesn't Paul condemn slavery or tell Philemon to free Onesimus?
hard.a:
This is the letter's hardest question, and its history makes it urgent. In the decades before the American Civil War, defenders of slavery cited Philemon as proof that the apostle returned a fugitive to his master and so approved the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 and the institution itself. Abolitionists answered that Paul sent Onesimus back "no longer as a slave" and "as a beloved brother", and that a master who took those words seriously could not keep treating a brother as property. Some went further and argued Onesimus had not been a slave at all. Enslaved Christians themselves often heard the Bible very differently from the way it was preached to them.

Several things can be said honestly. Paul was a prisoner with no power over Roman law, writing to a tiny community, and open calls for slaves to be freed could have brought violent suspicion on the church. He asks for more than the law required and hints at more than he asks (verse 21), and many scholars think he was requesting Onesimus's release. At the same time, he does not say that slavery is wrong, and readers should not pretend he does. The letter plants principles (a slave as a brother in the flesh and in the Lord, a master who owes his slave a welcome, equal standing in one church) that later Christians, from Gregory of Nyssa in the fourth century, who preached against slaveholding as such, to the evangelical abolitionists of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, drew out into a rejection of the institution. The church's slowness to draw that conclusion is part of its history to be confessed, not defended.

questions: Paul says he could command but chooses to appeal on the basis of love. When have you been changed more by someone's appeal than by an order?
Onesimus returns to the house he left, and Philemon must receive someone who wronged or embarrassed him. What makes that kind of reconciliation costly for both sides?
The letter was used both to defend and to oppose slavery. What does that history teach about reading the Bible in a way that protects our own interests?
